text:
Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swan. Today, should parents delay their child's surgery because the
anaesthetic might damage future school performance? Is there really as much
vitamin D deficiency around as some people say? With women living longer and
longer after a diagnosis of breast cancer, what support do they need? And new
and troubling findings about drug caused deaths amongst healthcare
professionals.

There's been lots of research suggesting that doctors and others are at increased
risk of suicide because of the stressful work, perhaps the kind of person attracted
to those professions, and the access to dangerous medications. But until this
study from the department of forensic medicine at Monash University, not much
has been known about Australian healthcare professionals, much less the full
range including paramedics, nurses and vets, as well as doctors and dentists.
And some of the results are quite surprising. The lead researcher was Jennifer
Pilgrim.

Jennifer Pilgrim: We looked at the deaths reported to an Australian coroner
between 2003 and 2013 where the death was caused by drugs and involved a
healthcare professional.

Norman Swan: And what did you find?

Jennifer Pilgrim: We found 404 deaths, most of these involved intentional self-
harm or suicide, and also mental illness. And professional and personal stresses
were also very common, so financial problems, relationship problems, workplace
stress, those sorts of things.

Norman Swan: These are cases that came to the coroner.

Jennifer Pilgrim: Yes, that's right, so these were all deaths that were reported to
the coroner…

Norman Swan: And you have any sense of what goes beyond that, how many
you might have missed that don't go to the coroner but might be deaths that are
self-harm?
 
Jennifer Pilgrim: All deaths that are unnatural or unexpected are reported to an
Australian coroner. So it should have captured all of these sorts of deaths, but
obviously it doesn't capture any of the living cases of drug abuse and intend to
self-harm in this population.

Norman Swan: So near misses and so on.

Jennifer Pilgrim: Yes.

Norman Swan: So what numbers did you come up with?

Jennifer Pilgrim: So there were 404 deaths altogether. Most of these involved
females and nurses. The rate of death which takes into account the number of
people employed in these professions in Australia was highest for the
veterinarian group, and most of these vets involved intentional self-harm where
they took an excessive amount or an overdose of barbiturates, which are drugs
commonly used in animal euthanasia.

Norman Swan: Did nurses come up top because there are far more nurses than
any other healthcare profession in Australia, or…

Jennifer Pilgrim: Exactly. I mean, there were more cases involving nurses,
however when we broke this down and put it in proportion of the number of
nurses as well as the other occupations working in these professions across
Australia, that's where the vets came up on top. So the veterinarian group was
smaller, but in proportion to the number of vets employed in Australia, the rate
was highest for vets.

Norman Swan: So let's dissect the gender split. So was it more women than
men because of the numbers of nurses, or that showed up in veterinarians as
well?

Jennifer Pilgrim: Exactly. There were more females in the cohort overall, but
obviously nursing is dominated by females and that was the largest category. So
when we looked at the doctors and other medical practitioners, men were highest
in this group. So I think the number of females is just the overrepresentation of
females in nursing.
 
Norman Swan: Before we get to the causes, it's been often said that
anaesthetists are a very common group within the medical profession who take
their own lives. Is that true in this group?

Jennifer Pilgrim: We did find a high mortality rate for the anaesthesiology group,
and most of these involved taking the anaesthetic drugs from work.

Norman Swan: And what about nursing specialty, did you manage to dissect
that further?

Jennifer Pilgrim: Because of the coding on the national coronial information
system database which we used for this research, some was more specific than
others, so we just looked at the nursing group as a whole. There were some that
were more specific that we could break down into the different groups, but we
tended just to just look at the group as a whole.

Norman Swan: This contradicts the national trend in suicide, does it not? I
mean, suicide, commoner in young males, commoner in elderly males, and
there's kind of a hollowed out group in the middle but generally completed suicide
is more common in men than in women, and you're turning up women. What's
going on here?

Jennifer Pilgrim: Well, that's a very good question. I think that it obviously is still
a problem in women, perhaps in the healthcare professional industry specifically.
So again, we had more women in this group because of the number of women in
nursing, but I guess it just raises the issue of suicide in this group among females
in this industry more specifically and why we need more research in this space.

Norman Swan: And with nurses it was access to the means as well as vets and
anaesthetists and others?

Jennifer Pilgrim: We found in about a fifth of the cases overall, the healthcare
professionals were accessing the drugs from work, so that included some
nurses, but that was just an overall figure. And of course this was where this had
actually been described in the coroner's findings. So it may have actually been
an underestimation of the true number of cases where people were accessing
drugs from work.
 
Norman Swan: Now, suicide is incredibly complicated. It's not necessarily
always related to mental health issues, can be impulsive, it can be for all sorts of
reasons. How good were the coroners in identifying what they thought were the
key factors leading to that person taking his or her own life?

Jennifer Pilgrim: That's something I probably won't be able to comment on
actually, I'm not an expert in suicide or coroner's findings, so I might just leave
that one for somebody else I think.

Norman Swan: But the factors that coroners did identify were what?

Jennifer Pilgrim: Yes, so the coroners, it sort of varies in cases and also the
coding of intentional self-harm on the national coronial information system
database is actually performed by coders interpreting the coronial findings.

Norman Swan: So in your view does this data…it's small numbers but each one
represents a major tragedy for the person and their loved ones around
them…does it tell you anything about prevention?

Jennifer Pilgrim: Well, I think one of the key findings of this study in terms of
prevention was that healthcare professionals are not exempt from mental illness
and substance abuse problems. I think that it would be easy to assume that they
are exempt from mental health and substance abuse problems but they are just
like everybody else. And what the research around the world shows us is that
many healthcare professionals are afraid to talk up and speak up about the
problems from the fear of stigmatisation and potentially losing their jobs. So,
many healthcare professionals either treat themselves or seek very private
treatment or don't seek treatment at all. So it just highlights the need for better
detection of these problems among healthcare professionals in order to provide
them with the support that they need.

Norman Swan: And do you have a theory about vets?

Jennifer Pilgrim: I don't actually. Our study didn't look into why vets were
overrepresented in terms of intentional self-harm. But other studies have
explored the higher prevalence of certain occupations in drug abuse and
intentional self-harm, and basically what they say is we are not really sure what
the answer is, whether it's environmental factors such as access to controlled
 
strokes and workplace stress, whether they are bigger contributors to this issue,
or whether certain individuals with a predisposition for drug abuse seek out these
professions.

Norman Swan: There is a bit of evidence that if you make it harder to get a hold
of a gun or you put up a fence on a spot where people traditionally have jumped
from, you do actually make a difference to the rates. And then when you actually
save people from an intention which would have definitely resulted in their death,
often there's regret and relief that in fact they were saved. What about restricting
access to the means?

Jennifer Pilgrim: That's really a question for the workplace and industries and
relevant regulation agencies for these professions, I can't comment on access to
drugs. But we are hopeful that this research helps to inform those policies and
helps to open up those avenues for discussion.

Norman Swan: Jennifer, thank you for joining us on the Health Report.

Jennifer Pilgrim: You're welcome.

Norman Swan: Jennifer Pilgrim is in the department of forensic medicine at
Monash University in Melbourne.

And you're listening to the Health Report here on RN, ABC news radio and CBC
radio across Canada.

Until the government changed the rules making vitamin D tests less enticing for
doctors to order, Australian taxpayers were spending hundreds of millions of
dollars a year on investigations which were mostly of little value. It was fuelled a
little bit by a panic generated by the belief that vitamin D deficiency was rife in the
community, despite all the sun shining on this big brown land. And now an article
in the prestigious New England Journal of Medicine has suggested that the case
for widespread vitamin D deficiency, at least in North America, has been
overblown. One of the authors is Professor Patsy Brannon from the department
of the nutritional sciences at Cornell University. Dr Brannon is speaking here to
Joel Werner who wanted to know will how vitamin D deficiency shows itself.
 
Patsy Brannon: Vitamin D deficiency is most recognised by its adverse impact
on bone health. So the deficiency in children can result in a condition known as
rickets, and in adults it can result in a condition known as osteomalacia. In both
conditions the bones are not well mineralised, so they are not as strong as you
would like them to be.

Joel Werner: But these symptoms only manifest in the most severe cases of
vitamin D deficiency. How do we measure vitamin D deficiency more generally?

Patsy Brannon: The way that we measure it is by measuring the amount of
metabolite, a form of vitamin D in our blood known as 25-hydroxy vitamin D, and
that tells us about not only the vitamin D that you get from your diet but the
vitamin D that you make in your skin when you are exposed to sunlight. So that
25-hydroxy D is really important for telling us what a person's complete exposure
to vitamin D is.

Joel Werner: But in an article you recently wrote in the New England Journal of
Medicine you suggest that maybe the way we've been measuring vitamin D has
problems. Can you dig into that a little bit for us?

Patsy Brannon: So it's not so much the measurement, it's how we interpret that
measurement. For this 25-hydroxy D, how much of it is too little and indicative of
being at risk for too little vitamin D or being vitamin D deficient? And how much of
it is the right amount to have. So if you have your vitamin D measured at your
doctor's office, they are going to tell you are you in the right range or do you have
too little, and are you at risk of being deficient? And the controversy has been
how do you judge, how do you interpret that 25-hydroxy D?

So in the United States and in other places, people have been using values of
more than 50 nanomoles per litre is optimal, and what they've been interpreting
then is anyone with values less than 50 nanomoles per litre is deficient. And our
article is about why that is not the best way to assess whether somebody has
enough vitamin D or too little vitamin D.

Joel Werner: And so why isn't that the best way to interpret these figures?

Patsy Brannon: Part of it gets at how you interpret the recommendations that
were made in the United States and Canada for how much vitamin D a healthy
 
population needs. And what that amount that's recommended is it meets the
needs of almost everybody in the population, 97.5% of the people in the
population. So in a way of thinking about how much nutrient you need, it also
means that some of our population needs less than that. So if you use that as a
cut point, if you say less than 50 nanomoles per litre is deficient, you are over-
estimating the prevalence of deficiency in your population.

Joel Werner: And the title of your article asks the question; is there really a
pandemic? So you're saying that by interpreting the measurements the way that
we have, we may have been overestimating the idea that there is a vitamin D
deficiency.

Patsy Brannon: We might be, yes. Based on the way that the recommended
amounts were determined in North America for US and Canada, what we would
want to look at is the number of people in our healthy population who have 25-
hydroxy D levels less than 40 nanomoles per litre. That becomes a much smaller
number. So, for example, in the US that's only 13% of our adults, not more than
30% of our adults.

Joel Werner: But what are the implications of not getting this right? Can you
describe why this is actually a problem?

Patsy Brannon: There is emerging evidence that there may be individuals that
have too much vitamin D. So we are seeing what has been referred to as a U-
shaped risk so that people who have very low vitamin D levels in their blood are
at risk for adverse bone health outcomes. But now we are seeing evidence that
people with higher levels of 25-hydroxy D in their blood may be at risk for some
cancers like pancreatic cancer, for an increased rate of falls. So now there's a
concern that we be in what we like to call in the US the sweet spot, so that we
don't have too little but we don't have too much.

Joel Werner: So what recommendation would you offer our listener out there
who is taking in this information, is saying, okay, I can have too much vitamin D, I
can have too little vitamin D, but what's the best advice that you'd give to
someone who is concerned about their level of vitamin D?

Patsy Brannon: So that's a really great question. In Australia you don't have a
lot of foods that are fortified with vitamin D. I think it's your low-fat table spreads,
 
the oil-based table spreads and margarines, a few dairy products but not very
many. So most of the vitamin D that you get in Australia is what you make in the
sun. And that becomes a concern because we know that UVB exposure
increases your lifetime risk for skin cancer. So there's another trade-off for you
that we are talking about. But also think about and talk with their physician about
how they expose themselves to the sun. So there are some recommendations in
Australia about sunlight exposure, although in the US our dermatologists are
adamant that you shouldn't be out in the sun without sunscreen. So that's a place
where I'd say talk to your physician. But look at the labels and think about what
foods you are choosing. And if you're going to take a vitamin D supplement to,
and many people do choose to do that, take one that has about 400 to 600 IUs a
day, which would be 10 to 15 micrograms per day.

Joel Werner: Professor Brannon, thanks for joining us on the Health
Report today.

Patsy Brannon: You're welcome, it was a pleasure speaking with you.

Norman Swan: Patsy Brannon, who is in the department of nutrition sciences at
Cornell University, and she was talking to the Health Report's Joel Werner.

There's been a theoretical concern that giving anaesthetics to children,
particularly young children, could be dangerous, and it comes from animal
studies which suggest some brain damage in neonatal animals when they are
exposed to modern anaesthetics. The question is, is this a real worry when it
comes to real human children? Well, that's been the subject of a very large study
in Queensland performed by Dr Pia Glatz and her colleagues. Pia Glatz is in the
department of anaesthesiology and intensive care medicine at Kalmar County
Hospital in Sweden. Welcome to the Health Report.

Pia Glatz: Thank you very much.

Norman Swan: So before you did your study, was there any evidence at all that
there was a worry in children?

Pia Glatz: We have very much evidence. As you said, many animal studies have
shown that all anaesthetic drugs we are using currently are neurotoxic, they give
brain damage when we give anaesthetic drugs to rat babies or monkey babies,
 
and of course that raises the question if this is applicable for human babies and
children.

Norman Swan: And has it ever been studied before you in children that it raises
a concern?

Pia Glatz: Yes, smaller studies, epidemiological studies just as ours. It's not so
easy to do these animal studies. For ethical reasons you can't just take a bunch
of kids and give them anaesthetic drugs and see what happens, so you have to
do it some other way.

Norman Swan: So what you do in your study?

Pia Glatz: In Sweden we have unique registers for the healthcare and school
systems, so we looked at all children born in Sweden between 1973 and 1993.
That's about 2 million children. And we found those who had surgery before age
4, and then we excluded those who had neurosurgery or serious malformation,
and surgery or medical diagnosis who we thought might affect cognitive
development.

Norman Swan: And what outcomes were you looking at? Was it just school
performance?

Pia Glatz: We looked after school grades, grades at age 16, that's when you
leave compulsory school in Sweden, and we also for the boys looked at the
intelligence tests all Swedish boys do when they are 18 and entering the military
system here.

Norman Swan: So I think you had 33,000 children out of the 2 million who had
had an anaesthetic. What did you find?

Pia Glatz: We found that those children compared to healthy children had 0.41%
lower school grades, so it's a statistically significant difference but it's very, very
small. We also looked at other factors that can affect school grades, and we
found that other factors affect it much more. If you are a boy you have 10% lower
school grades than girls, and if your mother lacks university education you have
10% lower school grades. And if you are born in December you have 6% lower
school grades than if you are born in January.
 
Norman Swan: Is that because you only get one present at Christmas instead of
two? Just being facetious. So what's the reason for December? Is that viral
infections in pregnancy or what?

Pia Glatz: I'm not sure, I think you are almost a year younger than your
classmates born in January, 11 months, I think that's the difference. We can see
a clear line, your grades get lower for every month you are born in February,
March, April it's a little lower school grades.

Norman Swan: And what about multiple surgeries? Some children, they fall a lot,
they need their fractures pinned or they've got a condition which requires multiple
surgeries.

Pia Glatz: We also looked at that. In the primary cohort we had 33,000 children,
we had only one surgery before aged four, and no subsequent hospitalisation for
whatever reason. And then we looked at those who had multiple surgery before
aged four, which was 3,000 or 4,000 children, and they had a little lower, about
1.5% or 1.8% lower school grades than those who did not. So maybe that's
because they had more duration of anaesthesia.

Norman Swan: And younger children versus older, if they were operated on in
infancy?

Pia Glatz: We thought that the youngest must be the most vulnerable, but we
couldn't find anything. On the contrary, we found that those who had lower school
grades were those who had their anaesthesia and surgery between 36 and 48
months. So we couldn't find that youngest theory to the six months were more
vulnerable.

Norman Swan: And I presume that you corrected for whether the baby was
premature and the condition that they might have had that might have affected
their development?

Pia Glatz: Yes, we have corrected for all factors we could think of. As I said,
Sweden has unique registers we have used, how many siblings you have, what
your mother's education is, if you are premature born, household incomes,
everything like that.
 
Norman Swan: And just finally, what does that mean then for parents whose
child might need to have an operation?

Pia Glatz: I would not be worried at all. We can see a small, small difference, but
it's so very small. Other factors affect school grades much more, and you also
have to take into account what happens if you don't do the surgery. We never
give surgery and anaesthesia to a child unless absolutely necessary, and you
have to think what happens if you don't do this maybe eye surgery or ear
surgery, that could give other problems.

Norman Swan: So common-sense prevails. Pia Glatz, thanks for joining us on
the Health Report.

Pia Glatz: Thanks for having me.

Norman Swan: Pia Glatz is in the department of anaesthetics and intensive care
at Kalmar County Hospital in Sweden, and we'll have a link to that paper on
the Health Report's website.

One of the great success stories…there aren't that many actually in cancer, but
one of the great success stories in cancer is breast cancer. For many women it
has become almost a chronic disease, so long do they live with the condition. But
that means that they live with the effects of treatment and perhaps require
supportive care, according to an article in today's Medical Journal of Australia.
And here to talk about it is one of the authors of that paper, Professor Fran Boyle
from the Mater Hospital in Sydney. Welcome to the Health Report.

Frances Boyle: Hi Norman.

Norman Swan: What are the issues that women with breast cancer face that
might need support?

Frances Boyle: Well, I think during treatment things like hair loss, for instance,
have been quite underestimated by health professionals in terms of the impact
they might have on a woman psychologically and her coping during treatment,
and that's something that we finally have some means to address for some
women undergoing chemotherapy, with scalp cooling. So that's something that's
 
new and which is widely used in the UK and Europe. So we're trying to make
sure that Australian women get better access to that.

Norman Swan: So this is like a cap where they run cold water through it so that
when the chemo is injected in it doesn't…the blood vessels are constricted in the
scalp and it doesn't go to the scalp as much as it would otherwise.

Frances Boyle: That's right, the hair follicles kind of hibernate and that means
that they are less affected by the chemo. And we know that women…and it's not
a vanity thing, it is often about trying to make sure that strangers in the
supermarket don't inspect the contents of your trolley and make suggestions
about organic food, or your children don't get distressed at the school gate when
you come to pick them up.

Norman Swan: And why aren't we using the skull caps?

Frances Boyle: Well, in Australia the funding for them has mainly been provided
through donations, and so that's a way that units are actually applying them, but
they do mean that patients spend more time in the chemotherapy unit. So if
you've got a very busy chemo unit, there's a lot of logistics that have to be
rearranged to make that work. But we've been working with different hospitals
around the country to see if we can solve problems for them, and gradually it's
spreading.

Norman Swan: A few weeks ago we were talking about what women should feel
entitled to when they've got breast cancer, and one is breast reconstruction, for
example, which they didn't really feel that way. Surely a woman is entitled to this
treatment.

Frances Boyle: I think it's something that has implications for the economics of
actually making chemotherapy manageable. So each unit needs to work out a
way to do that that makes sure other patients are not disadvantaged and waiting
lists aren't pushed out for other kinds of cancer. But I think most places in the
northern hemisphere it's considered to be standard of care. The US has of
course been slow to discover it but they are about to find out and it will become
normal.
 
Norman Swan: Another area which has been relatively neglected by the cancer
community is sexual well-being when you've had breast cancer.

Frances Boyle: I think that's right, Norman. At the first pass, people going
through treatment, the biggest concern is survival and making sure that their
treatment is accomplished on time and they get through that. Many women then
say, well, I thought it was okay to have no libido when I was having
chemotherapy or to have vaginal dryness when I first started my tablets, but you
know what, it's six months on and that's still an issue for me. And it's something
that oncologists or perhaps even surgeons are probably not the best in picking
up in their consultations, because again, follow-up consultations tend to focus on
recurrence risk.

Norman Swan: So this is more than just having had a mastectomy, although that
is increasingly rare in breast cancer, this is the effect of the treatment. And are
there ways of getting around this?

Frances Boyle: Well, we are learning ways to help women with these symptoms.
Libido is obviously a pretty complex concept that is not just a physical thing but
an emotional thing as well. But some of the vaginal symptoms to lend themselves
to treatment, and also making sure that women are referred for the right kind of
assessment and help with their partners is a really important thing to pick up on.

Norman Swan: One of the things that is underestimated also as time goes on is
distress. You think, well, a woman has survived for five years, surely she is not
distressed, but the distressed, anecdotally, when women come back for
surveillance and have their check-up seems to recur almost to as bad as it was
before.

Frances Boyle: I think that having that annual mammogram, women regularly
say while they are lying there having it or standing there, it's like being back at
the beginning all over again and it is now recognised that that is a form of post-
traumatic stress disorder and needs to be treated psychologically in a similar
way. So recent studies in Australia have shown that a psychological intervention
based on PTSD interventions is helpful for several kinds of cancer patients with
what's called fear of recurrence. And I would love to see that rolled out in a more
systematic way.
 
Norman Swan: So here we are, we are doling out expensive drugs in expensive
chemotherapy units, women are having treatment, surgical treatment…the
implication in your article is we've had this narrow focus on medical things, yet
you need this quite significant support infrastructure around women to actually
make the breast cancer care more humane and effective.

Frances Boyle: I think breast cancer has led the way, as you said, at improving
survival, and now most people will not die of breast cancer, they'll die of
something else. So it's a teachable moment, if you like, when other aspects of
their health can be addressed, particularly lifestyle factors such as diet and
exercise.

Norman Swan: But do the bean counters know they've got to pay for it?

Frances Boyle: Well, I think they prefer not to because a lot of that needs to be
delivered in the community. It's not really something that's easily delivered in
large public hospitals, it has to be close to where women live. And so really GPs
are going to be people who are perhaps in a better position to refer women to
local services.

Norman Swan: So it's a work in progress.

Frances Boyle: It's a work in progress, and I guess what we are hoping with this
article is that we will draw to attention, particularly of general practitioners, that
working together to solve these issues is going to be required, it's not something
that is going to happen just from the oncological community.

Norman Swan: Fran, thanks for joining us.

Frances Boyle: Thanks Norman.

Norman Swan: Frank Boyle is professor of medical oncology and director of the
Patricia Ritchie Centre for Cancer Care and Research at the Mater Hospital in
Sydney.

I'm Norman Swan, this has been the Health Report, hope you can join me next
week.

going on here?

Jennifer Pilgrim: Well, that's a very good question. I think that it obviously is still
a problem in women, perhaps in the healthcare professional industry specifically.
So again, we had more women in this group because of the number of women in
nursing, but I guess it just raises the issue of suicide in this group among females
in this industry more specifically and why we need more research in this space.

Norman Swan: And with nurses it was access to the means as well as vets and
anaesthetists and others?

Jennifer Pilgrim: We found in about a fifth of the cases overall, the healthcare
professionals were accessing the drugs from work, so that included some
nurses, but that was just an overall figure. And of course this was where this had
actually been described in the coroner's findings. So it may have actually been
an underestimation of the true number of cases where people were accessing
drugs from work.

Norman Swan: Now, suicide is incredibly complicated. It's not necessarily
always related to mental health issues, can be impulsive, it can be for all sorts of
reasons. How good were the coroners in identifying what they thought were the
key factors leading to that person taking his or her own life?

Jennifer Pilgrim: That's something I probably won't be able to comment on
actually, I'm not an expert in suicide or coroner's findings, so I might just leave
that one for somebody else I think.

Norman Swan: But the factors that coroners did identify were what?

Jennifer Pilgrim: Yes, so the coroners, it sort of varies in cases and also the
coding of intentional self-harm on the national coronial information system
database is actually performed by coders interpreting the coronial findings.

Norman Swan: So in your view does this data…it's small numbers but each one
represents a major tragedy for the person and their loved ones around
them…does it tell you anything about prevention?

Jennifer Pilgrim: Well, I think one of the key findings of this study in terms of
prevention was that healthcare professionals are not exempt from mental illness
and substance abuse problems. I think that it would be easy to assume that they
are exempt from mental health and substance abuse problems but they are just
like everybody else. And what the research around the world shows us is that
many healthcare professionals are afraid to talk up and speak up about the
problems from the fear of stigmatisation and potentially losing their jobs. So,
many healthcare professionals either treat themselves or seek very private
treatment or don't seek treatment at all. So it just highlights the need for better
detection of these problems among healthcare professionals in order to provide
them with the support that they need.

Norman Swan: And do you have a theory about vets?

Jennifer Pilgrim: I don't actually. Our study didn't look into why vets were
overrepresented in terms of intentional self-harm. But other studies have
explored the higher prevalence of certain occupations in drug abuse and
intentional self-harm, and basically what they say is we are not really sure what
the answer is, whether it's environmental factors such as access to controlled

strokes and workplace stress, whether they are bigger contributors to this issue,
or whether certain individuals with a predisposition for drug abuse seek out these
professions.

Norman Swan: There is a bit of evidence that if you make it harder to get a hold
of a gun or you put up a fence on a spot where people traditionally have jumped
from, you do actually make a difference to the rates. And then when you actually
save people from an intention which would have definitely resulted in their death,
often there's regret and relief that in fact they were saved. What about restricting
access to the means?

Jennifer Pilgrim: That's really a question for the workplace and industries and
relevant regulation agencies for these professions, I can't comment on access to
drugs. But we are hopeful that this research helps to inform those policies and
helps to open up those avenues for discussion.

Norman Swan: Jennifer, thank you for joining us on the Health Report.

Jennifer Pilgrim: You're welcome.

Norman Swan: Jennifer Pilgrim is in the department of forensic medicine at
Monash University in Melbourne.

And you're listening to the Health Report here on RN, ABC news radio and CBC
radio across Canada.

Until the government changed the rules making vitamin D tests less enticing for
doctors to order, Australian taxpayers were spending hundreds of millions of
dollars a year on investigations which were mostly of little value. It was fuelled a
little bit by a panic generated by the belief that vitamin D deficiency was rife in the
community, despite all the sun shining on this big brown land. And now an article
in the prestigious New England Journal of Medicine has suggested that the case
for widespread vitamin D deficiency, at least in North America, has been
overblown. One of the authors is Professor Patsy Brannon from the department
of the nutritional sciences at Cornell University. Dr Brannon is speaking here to
Joel Werner who wanted to know will how vitamin D deficiency shows itself.

Patsy Brannon: Vitamin D deficiency is most recognised by its adverse impact
on bone health. So the deficiency in children can result in a condition known as
rickets, and in adults it can result in a condition known as osteomalacia. In both
conditions the bones are not well mineralised, so they are not as strong as you
would like them to be.

Joel Werner: But these symptoms only manifest in the most severe cases of
vitamin D deficiency. How do we measure vitamin D deficiency more generally?

Patsy Brannon: The way that we measure it is by measuring the amount of
metabolite, a form of vitamin D in our blood known as 25-hydroxy vitamin D, and
that tells us about not only the vitamin D that you get from your diet but the
vitamin D that you make in your skin when you are exposed to sunlight. So that
25-hydroxy D is really important for telling us what a person's complete exposure
to vitamin D is.

Joel Werner: But in an article you recently wrote in the New England Journal of
Medicine you suggest that maybe the way we've been measuring vitamin D has
problems. Can you dig into that a little bit for us?

Patsy Brannon: So it's not so much the measurement, it's how we interpret that
measurement. For this 25-hydroxy D, how much of it is too little and indicative of
being at risk for too little vitamin D or being vitamin D deficient? And how much of
it is the right amount to have. So if you have your vitamin D measured at your
doctor's office, they are going to tell you are you in the right range or do you have
too little, and are you at risk of being deficient? And the controversy has been
how do you judge, how do you interpret that 25-hydroxy D?

So in the United States and in other places, people have been using values of
more than 50 nanomoles per litre is optimal, and what they've been interpreting
then is anyone with values less than 50 nanomoles per litre is deficient. And our
article is about why that is not the best way to assess whether somebody has
enough vitamin D or too little vitamin D.

Joel Werner: And so why isn't that the best way to interpret these figures?

Patsy Brannon: Part of it gets at how you interpret the recommendations that
were made in the United States and Canada for how much vitamin D a healthy

population needs. And what that amount that's recommended is it meets the
needs of almost everybody in the population, 97.5% of the people in the
population. So in a way of thinking about how much nutrient you need, it also
means that some of our population needs less than that. So if you use that as a
cut point, if you say less than 50 nanomoles per litre is deficient, you are over-
estimating the prevalence of deficiency in your population.

Joel Werner: And the title of your article asks the question; is there really a
pandemic? So you're saying that by interpreting the measurements the way that
we have, we may have been overestimating the idea that there is a vitamin D
deficiency.

Patsy Brannon: We might be, yes. Based on the way that the recommended
amounts were determined in North America for US and Canada, what we would
want to look at is the number of people in our healthy population who have 25-
hydroxy D levels less than 40 nanomoles per litre. That becomes a much smaller
number. So, for example, in the US that's only 13% of our adults, not more than
30% of our adults.

Joel Werner: But what are the implications of not getting this right? Can you
describe why this is actually a problem?

Patsy Brannon: There is emerging evidence that there may be individuals that
have too much vitamin D. So we are seeing what has been referred to as a U-
shaped risk so that people who have very low vitamin D levels in their blood are
at risk for adverse bone health outcomes. But now we are seeing evidence that
people with higher levels of 25-hydroxy D in their blood may be at risk for some
cancers like pancreatic cancer, for an increased rate of falls. So now there's a
concern that we be in what we like to call in the US the sweet spot, so that we
don't have too little but we don't have too much.

Joel Werner: So what recommendation would you offer our listener out there
who is taking in this information, is saying, okay, I can have too much vitamin D, I
can have too little vitamin D, but what's the best advice that you'd give to
someone who is concerned about their level of vitamin D?

Patsy Brannon: So that's a really great question. In Australia you don't have a
lot of foods that are fortified with vitamin D. I think it's your low-fat table spreads,

the oil-based table spreads and margarines, a few dairy products but not very
many. So most of the vitamin D that you get in Australia is what you make in the
sun. And that becomes a concern because we know that UVB exposure
increases your lifetime risk for skin cancer. So there's another trade-off for you
that we are talking about. But also think about and talk with their physician about
how they expose themselves to the sun. So there are some recommendations in
Australia about sunlight exposure, although in the US our dermatologists are
adamant that you shouldn't be out in the sun without sunscreen. So that's a place
where I'd say talk to your physician. But look at the labels and think about what
foods you are choosing. And if you're going to take a vitamin D supplement to,
and many people do choose to do that, take one that has about 400 to 600 IUs a
day, which would be 10 to 15 micrograms per day.

Joel Werner: Professor Brannon, thanks for joining us on the Health
Report today.

Patsy Brannon: You're welcome, it was a pleasure speaking with you.

Norman Swan: Patsy Brannon, who is in the department of nutrition sciences at
Cornell University, and she was talking to the Health Report's Joel Werner.

There's been a theoretical concern that giving anaesthetics to children,
particularly young children, could be dangerous, and it comes from animal
studies which suggest some brain damage in neonatal animals when they are
exposed to modern anaesthetics. The question is, is this a real worry when it
comes to real human children? Well, that's been the subject of a very large study
in Queensland performed by Dr Pia Glatz and her colleagues. Pia Glatz is in the
department of anaesthesiology and intensive care medicine at Kalmar County
Hospital in Sweden. Welcome to the Health Report.

Pia Glatz: Thank you very much.

Norman Swan: So before you did your study, was there any evidence at all that
there was a worry in children?

Pia Glatz: We have very much evidence. As you said, many animal studies have
shown that all anaesthetic drugs we are using currently are neurotoxic, they give
brain damage when we give anaesthetic drugs to rat babies or monkey babies,

and of course that raises the question if this is applicable for human babies and
children.

Norman Swan: And has it ever been studied before you in children that it raises
a concern?

Pia Glatz: Yes, smaller studies, epidemiological studies just as ours. It's not so
easy to do these animal studies. For ethical reasons you can't just take a bunch
of kids and give them anaesthetic drugs and see what happens, so you have to
do it some other way.

Norman Swan: So what you do in your study?

Pia Glatz: In Sweden we have unique registers for the healthcare and school
systems, so we looked at all children born in Sweden between 1973 and 1993.
That's about 2 million children. And we found those who had surgery before age
4, and then we excluded those who had neurosurgery or serious malformation,
and surgery or medical diagnosis who we thought might affect cognitive
development.

Norman Swan: And what outcomes were you looking at? Was it just school
performance?

Pia Glatz: We looked after school grades, grades at age 16, that's when you
leave compulsory school in Sweden, and we also for the boys looked at the
intelligence tests all Swedish boys do when they are 18 and entering the military
system here.

Norman Swan: So I think you had 33,000 children out of the 2 million who had
had an anaesthetic. What did you find?

Pia Glatz: We found that those children compared to healthy children had 0.41%
lower school grades, so it's a statistically significant difference but it's very, very
small. We also looked at other factors that can affect school grades, and we
found that other factors affect it much more. If you are a boy you have 10% lower
school grades than girls, and if your mother lacks university education you have
10% lower school grades. And if you are born in December you have 6% lower
school grades than if you are born in January.

Norman Swan: Is that because you only get one present at Christmas instead of
two? Just being facetious. So what's the reason for December? Is that viral
infections in pregnancy or what?

Pia Glatz: I'm not sure, I think you are almost a year younger than your
classmates born in January, 11 months, I think that's the difference. We can see
a clear line, your grades get lower for every month you are born in February,
March, April it's a little lower school grades.

Norman Swan: And what about multiple surgeries? Some children, they fall a lot,
they need their fractures pinned or they've got a condition which requires multiple
surgeries.

Pia Glatz: We also looked at that. In the primary cohort we had 33,000 children,
we had only one surgery before aged four, and no subsequent hospitalisation for
whatever reason. And then we looked at those who had multiple surgery before
aged four, which was 3,000 or 4,000 children, and they had a little lower, about
1.5% or 1.8% lower school grades than those who did not. So maybe that's
because they had more duration of anaesthesia.

Norman Swan: And younger children versus older, if they were operated on in
infancy?

Pia Glatz: We thought that the youngest must be the most vulnerable, but we
couldn't find anything. On the contrary, we found that those who had lower school
grades were those who had their anaesthesia and surgery between 36 and 48
months. So we couldn't find that youngest theory to the six months were more
vulnerable.

Norman Swan: And I presume that you corrected for whether the baby was
premature and the condition that they might have had that might have affected
their development?

Pia Glatz: Yes, we have corrected for all factors we could think of. As I said,
Sweden has unique registers we have used, how many siblings you have, what
your mother's education is, if you are premature born, household incomes,
everything like that.

Norman Swan: And just finally, what does that mean then for parents whose
child might need to have an operation?

Pia Glatz: I would not be worried at all. We can see a small, small difference, but
it's so very small. Other factors affect school grades much more, and you also
have to take into account what happens if you don't do the surgery. We never
give surgery and anaesthesia to a child unless absolutely necessary, and you
have to think what happens if you don't do this maybe eye surgery or ear
surgery, that could give other problems.

Norman Swan: So common-sense prevails. Pia Glatz, thanks for joining us on
the Health Report.

Pia Glatz: Thanks for having me.

Norman Swan: Pia Glatz is in the department of anaesthetics and intensive care
at Kalmar County Hospital in Sweden, and we'll have a link to that paper on
the Health Report's website.

One of the great success stories…there aren't that many actually in cancer, but
one of the great success stories in cancer is breast cancer. For many women it
has become almost a chronic disease, so long do they live with the condition. But
that means that they live with the effects of treatment and perhaps require
supportive care, according to an article in today's Medical Journal of Australia.
And here to talk about it is one of the authors of that paper, Professor Fran Boyle
from the Mater Hospital in Sydney. Welcome to the Health Report.

Frances Boyle: Hi Norman.

Norman Swan: What are the issues that women with breast cancer face that
might need support?

Frances Boyle: Well, I think during treatment things like hair loss, for instance,
have been quite underestimated by health professionals in terms of the impact
they might have on a woman psychologically and her coping during treatment,
and that's something that we finally have some means to address for some
women undergoing chemotherapy, with scalp cooling. So that's something that's

new and which is widely used in the UK and Europe. So we're trying to make
sure that Australian women get better access to that.

Norman Swan: So this is like a cap where they run cold water through it so that
when the chemo is injected in it doesn't…the blood vessels are constricted in the
scalp and it doesn't go to the scalp as much as it would otherwise.

Frances Boyle: That's right, the hair follicles kind of hibernate and that means
that they are less affected by the chemo. And we know that women…and it's not
a vanity thing, it is often about trying to make sure that strangers in the
supermarket don't inspect the contents of your trolley and make suggestions
about organic food, or your children don't get distressed at the school gate when
you come to pick them up.

Norman Swan: And why aren't we using the skull caps?

Frances Boyle: Well, in Australia the funding for them has mainly been provided
through donations, and so that's a way that units are actually applying them, but
they do mean that patients spend more time in the chemotherapy unit. So if
you've got a very busy chemo unit, there's a lot of logistics that have to be
rearranged to make that work. But we've been working with different hospitals
around the country to see if we can solve problems for them, and gradually it's
spreading.

Norman Swan: A few weeks ago we were talking about what women should feel
entitled to when they've got breast cancer, and one is breast reconstruction, for
example, which they didn't really feel that way. Surely a woman is entitled to this
treatment.

Frances Boyle: I think it's something that has implications for the economics of
actually making chemotherapy manageable. So each unit needs to work out a
way to do that that makes sure other patients are not disadvantaged and waiting
lists aren't pushed out for other kinds of cancer. But I think most places in the
northern hemisphere it's considered to be standard of care. The US has of
course been slow to discover it but they are about to find out and it will become
normal.

Norman Swan: Another area which has been relatively neglected by the cancer
community is sexual well-being when you've had breast cancer.

Frances Boyle: I think that's right, Norman. At the first pass, people going
through treatment, the biggest concern is survival and making sure that their
treatment is accomplished on time and they get through that. Many women then
say, well, I thought it was okay to have no libido when I was having
chemotherapy or to have vaginal dryness when I first started my tablets, but you
know what, it's six months on and that's still an issue for me. And it's something
that oncologists or perhaps even surgeons are probably not the best in picking
up in their consultations, because again, follow-up consultations tend to focus on
recurrence risk.

Norman Swan: So this is more than just having had a mastectomy, although that
is increasingly rare in breast cancer, this is the effect of the treatment. And are
there ways of getting around this?

Frances Boyle: Well, we are learning ways to help women with these symptoms.
Libido is obviously a pretty complex concept that is not just a physical thing but
an emotional thing as well. But some of the vaginal symptoms to lend themselves
to treatment, and also making sure that women are referred for the right kind of
assessment and help with their partners is a really important thing to pick up on.

Norman Swan: One of the things that is underestimated also as time goes on is
distress. You think, well, a woman has survived for five years, surely she is not
distressed, but the distressed, anecdotally, when women come back for
surveillance and have their check-up seems to recur almost to as bad as it was
before.

Frances Boyle: I think that having that annual mammogram, women regularly
say while they are lying there having it or standing there, it's like being back at
the beginning all over again and it is now recognised that that is a form of post-
traumatic stress disorder and needs to be treated psychologically in a similar
way. So recent studies in Australia have shown that a psychological intervention
based on PTSD interventions is helpful for several kinds of cancer patients with
what's called fear of recurrence. And I would love to see that rolled out in a more
systematic way.

Norman Swan: So here we are, we are doling out expensive drugs in expensive
chemotherapy units, women are having treatment, surgical treatment…the
implication in your article is we've had this narrow focus on medical things, yet
you need this quite significant support infrastructure around women to actually
make the breast cancer care more humane and effective.

Frances Boyle: I think breast cancer has led the way, as you said, at improving
survival, and now most people will not die of breast cancer, they'll die of
something else. So it's a teachable moment, if you like, when other aspects of
their health can be addressed, particularly lifestyle factors such as diet and
exercise.

Norman Swan: But do the bean counters know they've got to pay for it?

Frances Boyle: Well, I think they prefer not to because a lot of that needs to be
delivered in the community. It's not really something that's easily delivered in
large public hospitals, it has to be close to where women live. And so really GPs
are going to be people who are perhaps in a better position to refer women to
local services.

Norman Swan: So it's a work in progress.

Frances Boyle: It's a work in progress, and I guess what we are hoping with this
article is that we will draw to attention, particularly of general practitioners, that
working together to solve these issues is going to be required, it's not something
that is going to happen just from the oncological community.

Norman Swan: Fran, thanks for joining us.

Frances Boyle: Thanks Norman.

Norman Swan: Frank Boyle is professor of medical oncology and director of the
Patricia Ritchie Centre for Cancer Care and Research at the Mater Hospital in
Sydney.

I'm Norman Swan, this has been the Health Report, hope you can join me next
week.
